message.content: Aluminum conducts heat faster than cast iron, which is why a thin aluminum pan warms up almost immediately. But conducting heat and storing heat are different jobs. Cast iron is much denser and heavier, so a typical skillet contains far more metal. That gives it greater thermal mass: it takes more energy to change its temperature, and it releases that stored energy more slowly. In practice, preheat a cast-iron skillet and sear a steak. When the cool meat hits the surface, the heavy pan has enough stored heat to keep the surface sizzling and build a brown crust. A thin aluminum pan may lose its heat quickly at the contact point and cool down, even though heat moves through the aluminum fast. One limitation: this comparison assumes similar pan size and thickness. A thick aluminum pan, or one with a heavy base, can store plenty of heat too, and a very thin cast-iron pan would not stay hot as long. Also, cast iron’s slow response means it adjusts sluggishly when you change the burner.
